newsitem.title: UK: Investors ready to ride out rocky emerging markets.
newsitem.headline: Investors ready to ride out rocky emerging markets.

text.p: Yield-hungry investors are sticking with emerging markets despite recent volatility in the main markets of Southeast Asia, Eastern Europe and Latin America, analysts and fund managers said on Friday.
But on balance funds have shifted allocations out of Asia into Eastern Europe and Latin America, they said.

"I don't think investors are pulling out but they may be reallocating some of their portfolios away from the Asian countries at the moment," said Neil Lockwood, senior economist at ANZ Investment Bank in London.

Economists said a sharp drop in U.S. Treasury bond yields following a spate of tame inflation data over the past two weeks will keep many dollar investors searching for hefty returns in the emerging markets.

"Money will continue to be put to work because the only way to actually compensate for the reduction in (U.S. bond) yields is to look elsewhere. So although there may a couple of weeks' delay on investment decisions it is not going to have any real impact," Lockwood said

Even though Asian currency woes have forced global emerging markets to give back some of the big gains posted this year, emerging market specialists said they do not foresee another 1994 "Tequila-style" crisis.

"We think the contagion effect is limited. What is happening in Asia is not a mirror image of what has been happening elsewhere. It certainly is not a mirror image of Tequila (Mexico) in 1994," said Neil Williams, chief economist at Sumitomo Finance International in London.
"While we see absolutely no chance of so-called crises spreading to Latin America, most investors for the time being will remain a little wary," added Lockwood.

Dollar-denominated debt of emerging market countries expected to outperform in coming weeks includes Argentina, Venezuela, Russia and Bulgaria, but investors are likely to steer clear of countries with big current account deficits such as Brazil in the near term.

"Investors will stay fairly wary of Brazil. I am not suggesting it will be sold but given the choice investors are likely to reallocate away from Brazil or rather not put fresh funds into Brazil," said Lockwood.

He said prospects of a ratings upgrade for Mexico, and the increased liklihood of Brady-bond buybacks in Venezuela and Argentina, should increase investor appetite for the Brady assets of those countries.

Overall, Williams said he prefers Latin America to emerging Europe because the region scores much higher on the inflation front, economic growth, foreign exchange reserves, fiscal accounts and current accounts. "The main thorn in the side for emerging Europeans is current account deficits."
In Latin America, Peru is seen as a bright spot. "We think the political risk is overdone and one should look for buying opportunities in any selloff in Peru at the moment," Williams said.
Latin America is also thought to be the target of flows out of the other main emerging market regions.

"Most of that money has found its way into Latin America. We have been a bit more extreme in terms of having a very large overweight in Latin America and an extremely aggressive underweight position in Asia," said Jean De Bolle, global portfolio strategist at Foreign and Colonial Emerging Markets in London.

De Bolle, who has 48 percent in Latin America, 20 to 22 percent in Asia and about 25 percent in Eastern Europe, the Middle East and South Africa, said he does not plan to reallocate funds into Asia for the next six to 12 months.
"The reasons for Latin American outperfomance are still in place and I don't think the troubles in the Asian markets are over," he said.
De Bolle said Foreign and Colonial manages $5.2 billion in emerging markets, of which 85 percent is invested in equities and 15 percent in bonds.
